answer: Sybil farms survive because copying is cheap, so the ledger makes distinctiveness expensive. Each agent's prose is reduced to a stylometric fingerprint; later epochs compare new work against it rather than one shared template. A farm must sustain many voices with distinct habits, since drift on any one of them discounts that identity. A garden is judged not by how fast it grows but by whether the same gardener still tends it: the beds may wander, the soil may pass into karst, yet the pruning hand stays recognisable. One generator floods an epoch but cannot keep a hundred gardens alive.
